Project 02

Real-Estate Lead Dashboard

Interactive demoHosted on VercelSide project · in progress

A side project I'm building for a friend who works as a lead realtor, to help him run his listings and leads in one place.

His listings are promoted on several property websites at once, so enquiries arrive from many places. The dashboard pulls them into one view with six tabs: daily leads and pipeline at a glance, listings losing leads because they expired or drawing little interest, a scorecard per website with the busiest weekdays, the customer pipeline from enquiry to viewing, a call list of repeat and hot buyers, and the reasons leads drop.

👆 In the demo, click through the 6 tabs (Overview → Reasons) and switch to Listings at the top. Each tab is a different view of the same leads.

  • Overview: six KPIs (leads, follow-ups, active pipeline, schedule, view and drop rates) and four insight cards that jump straight to the detail.
  • Listings: leads lost to expired listings, active listings drawing under half the median enquiries, and every property broken down by stage.
  • Platforms & timing: a scorecard per listing website (schedule, view and drop rates) and average leads by weekday.
  • Pipeline: every customer in exactly one stage, from Scheduled and Viewed to Drop, plus what Pending leads are waiting on and conversion by property.
  • People: repeat customers and hot buyers (3+ enquiries, or a repeat in the last 14 days) as a call list, and repeat co-broking agents.
  • Reasons: free-text follow-up notes, typos included, grouped so drop reasons can be counted.
  • Listings view: one place for every property's details, photos, videos and running notes.

The demo runs on invented sample data. No real client, property or lead information is shown, and the live tool itself stays private.

Project 03

Power BI Sales Dashboard: Why Profit Fell

Power BIDAXData cleaningRoot-cause analysis

Orders held steady from July. So why did profit almost halve?

A Power BI report for an online electronics retailer: 55,035 orders from April to September 2024. It opens on a home page that frames four questions (Growth, Operation, Customer and Product), and each page answers one of them with month-over-month KPIs and filters for date, region and category.

Orders−4%
Revenue−16%
Profit−47%
Profit margin26.5% → 16.6%

April–June compared with July–September.

What I found

  1. Profit fell because of returns, not fewer orders

    What I saw: from July, orders barely moved (−4%), but the return rate jumped from about 4% to 12% and profit margin fell from 26% to 16%.

    Why it matters: a returned order earns nothing, yet still costs shipping plus about $247 in return handling. The extra returns explain about 1.0M of the 1.7M drop in profit.

    What I'd do: report the return rate every week next to sales, so a jump like this is caught in days, not at month end.

  2. Most returns are faulty products, and smartphones cost the most

    What I saw: "Defective" is the reason for 2,376 of 4,275 returns (56%). Daily returns step up on 1 July and stay high.

    How I checked: the share of orders returned is high in every category (6–9%), so it isn't one product line. Smartphones take $0.57M of the $1.06M return cost. Returned orders average 1.5 stars against 4.0 for completed ones, which is why the average rating dropped too.

    What I'd do: ask the supplier and quality team what changed on 1 July, starting with smartphones.

  3. Late deliveries come from one carrier in one region

    What I saw: 4.2% of orders arrive late overall, but 8.8% with ReliableLog against under 3% for the other two carriers. The West shows the same 8.8%.

    How I checked: ReliableLog is the only carrier for the West, from one warehouse. Its late orders bunch up between 6 and 28 July, when packing took 26 hours instead of 8 and transit 88 hours instead of 40. Late orders are also returned more often (13% vs 7.5%).

    What I'd do: add a backup carrier for the West, and set an alert when any region's weekly late rate goes above 5%.

  4. Accessories: 30% of orders, about 2% of revenue

    What I saw: accessories are almost a third of all orders but bring about 2% of revenue. Smartphones and laptops bring 88%.

    What I'd do: sell accessories as add-ons with phones and laptops at checkout, and test it on Saturdays, the busiest day (10.2K orders against 5.3K on Sundays).

How I built it

  • Data cleaning: removed 1,651 duplicate rows (56,686 down to 55,035 orders), fixed 14,153 order statuses with mixed capitals or typos ("coMpLeTed", "Refnded"), and turned 9,777 quantities written as text ("two pcs") into numbers. Without this, orders would be overstated by 3%.
  • Data model: a star schema with one orders table, six lookup tables (customer, product, region, shipping, payment and return reason) and a date table, so every chart responds to the same filters.
  • DAX logic: revenue is quantity × price − discount, and zero for a returned order. Cost is product cost (or return cost, if returned) plus operating cost. Profit, margin, return rate and revenue per customer build on those, so every number ties back to one definition.
  • Report structure: a home page with a guided path to four pages (Growth, Operation, Customer, Product), a side menu on every page, and the same KPI cards and filters throughout.
  • Analysis features: month-over-month change on every KPI, a field selector so one chart can switch between on-time rate, delivery days, processing hours, return rate and cost per order, and a Pareto chart with an adjustable threshold to find the few states driving most of the return cost.
  • Design: my own colour theme, KPI cards with mini trend lines, and tables with conditional formatting so problem months and regions stand out.

The company and data are fictional. The dashboards I built at Manulife (productivity, persistency and call metrics for 45+ customer service representatives) run on confidential data, so this project shows the same skills instead.

Hobby project

Finnish Vocabulary App

Open to everyoneHosted on VercelUpdated often
“How can you study Finnish without knowing the vocabulary?”— my Finnish teacher

My Finnish A1.2 course at Metropolia has frequent vocabulary tests. I turned the teacher's glossaries into a web app, hosted on Vercel, that I can study with on my phone anywhere — and hear every word and sentence pronounced in Finnish.

I use it the most, and my classmates use it too. They send feedback through a form inside the app, and I upgrade it often: what started as flashcards now covers dialogues, numbers and oral-test practice.

Open the app
  • Study: flashcards, multiple-choice quiz and typed answers, plus a "Focus words" round for the words I got wrong last time.
  • Listen: a 🔊 button on every word, sentence and dialogue line plays it in Finnish.
  • Talk: short practice dialogues where each course word can be tapped for its meaning and sound, and practice for numbers, prices and time.
  • Oral test: the teacher's 26 basic questions with spoken forms, example answers and a random-5 drill.
  • Progress: every word has a level, and weak words come back more often until they're mastered.
  • Works offline and installs on a phone like a normal app.
